**Table 1.1.** Different coefficients and exponents used to calculate formation factor (*F*). (Modified after Asquith, 1980.)

| *a*: Tortousity factor | *m*: Cementation exponent | Comments |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 2.0 | Carbonates¹ |
| 0.81 | 2.0 | Consolidated sandstones¹ |
| 0.62 | 2.15 | Unconsolidated sands (Humble formula)¹ |
| 1.45 | 1.54 | Average sands (after Carothers, 1968) |
| 1.65 | 1.33 | Shaly sands (after Carothers, 1968) |
| 1.45 | 1.70 | Calcareous sands (after Carothers, 1968) |
| 0.85 | 2.14 | Carbonates (after Carothers, 1968) |
| 2.45 | 1.08 | Pliocene sands, southern California (after Carothers and Porter, 1970) |
| 1.97 | 1.29 | Miocene sands, Texas–Louisiana Gulf Coast (after Carothers and Porter, 1970) |
| 1.0 | φ^(2.05-φ) | Clean granular formations (after Sethi, 1979) |

¹Most commonly used

variables: A = cross-sectional area of substance being measured (m^2)
L = length of substance being measured (m)
R_o = resistivity of a water-filled formation
R_w = resistivity of the water filling the formation
m = cementation exponent whose value varies with grain size, grain-size distribution, and the complexity of the paths between pores (tortuosity)
a = tortuosity factor, commonly set to 1.0
n = saturation exponent, typically 1.8 to 2.5, most commonly assumed to be 2
